# Research: PR/FAQ citation audit — OpenClaw CVEs, LangChain survey, Cisco privacy study, GitHub star counts

**Date:** 2026-08-29
**Request:** Peer-review citation audit of `prfaq.tex` — verify/correct 5 flagged claims: CVE-2026-25253, CVE-2026-24763 (and the ClawHub malicious-skills claim currently fused with it), the LangChain "78%/51%" adoption stat, the Cisco 2025 Data Privacy Benchmark "64%" stat, and current GitHub star counts for AutoGPT and OpenClaw/ClawdBot.
**Claims investigated:** 6 (item 2 splits into a CVE claim and a separate supply-chain claim)

## Evidence Found

**Claim**: CVE-2026-25253 (CVSS 8.8) "allowed gateway compromise via authentication bypass in misconfigured reverse proxies"
**Verdict**: CONTRADICTED
**Sources**:
- [SOCRadar: CVE-2026-25253: 1-Click RCE in OpenClaw Through Auth Token Exfiltration](https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-25253-rce-openclaw-auth-token/) — primary technical writeup: OpenClaw's Control UI trusts an attacker-controlled `gatewayUrl` query-string parameter with no origin validation or allowlisting, auto-connects a WebSocket on page load, and sends the stored gateway auth token in the connect payload. An attacker lures the victim to a malicious link, captures the token via cross-site WebSocket hijacking, reconnects to the real gateway with the stolen token, disables the sandbox (`exec.approvals.set = off`), escapes the Docker container (`tools.exec.host = gateway`), and achieves full host RCE.
- [The Hacker News: OpenClaw Bug Enables One-Click Remote Code Execution via Malicious Link](https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/openclaw-bug-enables-one-click-remote.html) — secondary confirmation, same attack chain, disclosed 2026-01-26, patched in v2026.1.29 (2026-01-30).
- GitHub Security Advisory [GHSA-g8p2-7wf7-98mq](https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/clawdbot/CVE-2026-25253/) — official advisory.
**Contradictory evidence**: None found supporting the doc's "reverse proxy" / "misconfigured proxy" framing — no source describes this vulnerability as proxy-related. The doc's description is a mischaracterization, not a simplification.
**Recommendation**: Replace the doc's description in full. Corrected text: "CVE-2026-25253 (CVSS 8.8) was a one-click RCE: OpenClaw's Control UI trusted an unvalidated `gatewayUrl` query parameter, auto-connected a WebSocket to it, and leaked the operator's gateway auth token in the connect payload — enabling cross-site WebSocket hijacking, sandbox-disable, and Docker escape to full host compromise from a single malicious link."

---

**Claim**: CVE-2026-24763 "enabled hundreds of malicious skills in the skill directory"
**Verdict**: CONTRADICTED (the CVE is unrelated to the malicious-skills issue; the malicious-skills issue is real but is a separate, uncredentialed supply-chain finding)
**Sources**:
- [GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-mc68-q9jw-2h3v: Command Injection in Clawdbot Docker Execution via PATH Environment Variable](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/security/advisories/GHSA-mc68-q9jw-2h3v) — CWE-78 command injection. Prior to v2026.1.29, OpenClaw's Docker sandbox execution built shell commands by unsafely interpolating the `PATH` environment variable. An *authenticated* user able to control environment variables could inject commands, achieving container compromise. No connection to the skill directory.
- [Tenable: CVE-2026-24763](https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-24763) and [SentinelOne: CVE-2026-24763](https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-24763/) — corroborate the PATH/Docker/command-injection description; fixed in v2026.1.29 by moving user input from the command string to environment variables (data channel vs. code channel).
**Contradictory evidence**: No source ties CVE-2026-24763 to the skill directory or ClawHub in any way.
**Recommendation**: Split into two separate cited claims (see below).

**Corrected CVE-2026-24763 text**: "CVE-2026-24763 was an authenticated command-injection flaw (CWE-78) in OpenClaw's Docker sandbox execution: unsafe handling of the `PATH` environment variable let an authenticated user inject shell commands and compromise the container. Fixed in v2026.1.29."

---

**Claim** (the malicious-skills supply-chain issue, needs its own citation): "hundreds of malicious skills in the skill directory"
**Verdict**: SUPPORTED (as a distinct, uncredentialed finding — not a CVE)
**Sources**:
- [Dark Reading: More Malicious OpenClaw Skills Threaten AI Supply Chain](https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/malicious-openclaw-skills-clawhub-threaten-ai-supply-chain)
- [Koi Security research, via eSecurity Planet: Hundreds of Malicious Skills Found in OpenClaw's ClawHub](https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/hundreds-of-malicious-skills-found-in-openclaws-clawhub/) — primary research by Oren Yomtov (Koi Security): audited all 2,857 skills on ClawHub (OpenClaw's skill marketplace) and found 341 malicious entries (11.9% of the registry). 335 of those traced to one coordinated campaign, "ClawHavoc," which distributed infostealer payloads (Atomic macOS Stealer / AMOS) via skills targeting cryptocurrency wallets, browser credentials, and SSH keys — estimated to target ~300,000 OpenClaw users.
- [Unit 42: OpenClaw's Skill Marketplace and the Emerging AI Supply Chain Threat](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/) — follow-on Palo Alto Networks research, later found additional malicious skills evading ClawHub's post-incident screening.
- [SlowMist: Threat Intelligence — Analysis of ClawHub Malicious Skills Poisoning](https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-analysis-of-clawhub-malicious-skills-poisoning-0448ffd49c80)
**Contradictory evidence**: None — this is a well-corroborated, multi-source finding, distinct from both CVEs above. Note it is NOT a CVE; it is a marketplace/supply-chain vetting failure (ClawHub had no comprehensive review process at the time).
**Recommendation**: Cite separately from CVE-2026-24763. Corrected text: "Separately, a February 2026 Koi Security audit found 341 malicious skills among the 2,857 published on ClawHub, OpenClaw's skill marketplace (11.9% of the registry) — most traced to a single campaign, ClawHavoc, distributing infostealer malware targeting cryptocurrency wallets and credentials to an estimated 300,000 OpenClaw users."

---

**Claim**: LangChain "78% planning to deploy agents soon" (2024 State of AI Agents report) alongside "51% in production"
**Verdict**: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — the reviewer's claim that 78% is mid-sized-company-specific is INCORRECT; the doc's original figure is accurate to the 2024 report. However, a newer, more current 2025 survey exists and should be added/considered as a supersede.
**Sources**:
- [LangChain: State of AI Agents Report (2024)](https://www.langchain.com/stateofaiagents) — exact quoted text (verified via WebFetch and cross-checked against secondary quotes): "51% of respondents are using agents in production today. 78% have active plans to implement agents into production soon." This 78% figure applies to the **whole survey sample** (1,300+ professionals), not a mid-sized-company subset. The mid-sized-company-specific (100–2000 employees) figure is 63% *already in production* — a different statistic entirely.
- [InfoQ: AI agents langchain (Dec 2024)](https://www.infoq.com/news/2024/12/ai-agents-langchain) — corroborates: "51% of respondents currently use AI agents in production, with mid-sized companies leading the way at 63%... 78% of participants reported plans to implement agents in the near future" (whole-sample framing for 78%).
- [LangChain: State of Agent Engineering (2025/2026 survey)](https://www.langchain.com/state-of-agent-engineering) — newer survey, ran Nov 18–Dec 2, 2025, n=1,340. Finding: 57.3% of respondents now have agents in production (up from 51% the year before), with another 30.4% actively developing agents with concrete deployment plans. Enterprise-size breakdown: 67% of 10k+-employee orgs have agents in production vs. 50% of <100-employee orgs.
**Contradictory evidence**: The reviewer's specific claim that "78% is mid-sized-company-specific" is not borne out by the primary source's own text — it is a whole-sample figure. The reviewer is correct, however, that a newer, more current survey with a different (and higher) production number exists and is not currently cited.
**Recommendation**: Two options. (a) Keep the 2024 stat as-is (it is accurate as characterized) but add the 2025 survey as a second, more current data point — cite both, noting the 2025 figure supersedes/updates the 2024 one: "up from 51% in the prior LangChain survey." (b) Replace entirely with the 2025 figure if the doc wants the single most current number: "57.3% of AI-agent teams now have agents in production, per LangChain's November–December 2025 survey of 1,340 practitioners — up from 51% the year prior." Do not describe 78% as mid-sized-specific; that would introduce a new inaccuracy.

---

**Claim**: Cisco 2025 Data Privacy Benchmark — "64% worry about exposing sensitive data to cloud GenAI tools"
**Verdict**: CONTRADICTED on wording (the 64% figure is not "cloud"-specific); the doc also omits a directly relevant contrasting finding (91% trust global providers).
**Sources**:
- [Cisco Newsroom: Cisco's 2025 Data Privacy Benchmark Study](https://newsroom.cisco.com/c/r/newsroom/en/us/a/y2025/m04/cisco-2025-data-privacy-benchmark-study-privacy-landscape-grows-increasingly-complex-in-the-age-of-ai.html) — primary source, published 2026-04-02 [sic, dated 2025-04-02 per URL], 2,600+ privacy/security professionals across 12 countries. Exact finding: 64% worry about **inadvertently sharing sensitive information publicly or with competitors** — a general concern about GenAI tool usage, not specifically about "cloud" GenAI tools as distinct from local/on-device GenAI. The study separately reports 90% of organizations see local data storage as inherently safer, AND (a different, contrasting finding) 91% trust global providers for better data protection (up 5 points year-over-year) — the report frames this as a live tension/paradox in the industry, not a one-sided "cloud is scary" finding.
- [Cisco investor relations PDF: same study](https://investor.cisco.com/files/doc_news/Ciscos-2025-Data-Privacy-Benchmark-Study-Privacy-landscape-grows-increasingly-complex-in-the-age-of-AI-2025.pdf) — corroborates.
**Contradictory evidence**: The doc's own bib entry (`cisco2025privacy`, already in `prfaq.bib`) actually has the correct note text ("90% see local storage as safer; 64% worry about cloud GenAI data exposure") — so the bib note itself also needs correcting, not just the `.tex` prose, if the bib note is being treated as source of truth. The 91% figure is currently omitted from both the `.tex` prose and the `.bib` note.
**Recommendation**: Revise the doc's sentence to remove the "cloud" qualifier and add the 91%-trust counterpoint for balance, since PR/FAQ risk analysis benefits from showing the full tension rather than a one-sided stat. Corrected text: "Cisco's 2025 Data Privacy Benchmark Study found 64% of respondents worry about inadvertently sharing sensitive information publicly or with competitors via GenAI tools, even as 90% see local data storage as inherently safer — though the same study found 91% trust global cloud providers for better data protection than they could provide themselves, up 5 points year-over-year, showing the market is genuinely split rather than uniformly local-preferring." Also update the `.bib` note for `cisco2025privacy` to match.

---

**Claim**: AutoGPT has "182,000+" GitHub stars (as of ~Feb 2026 per doc)
**Verdict**: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — was plausible for Feb 2026, but stale as of now (2026-08-29/30).
**Sources**:
- Direct fetch of [github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT](https://github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT) — current count (checked 2026-08-29) is approximately **187,000 stars** ("187.0k stars" displayed), 46,049 forks. A separately queried metrics snapshot (dated commit activity through 2026-08-20) reported 186,694 stars.
**Contradictory evidence**: None — this is simply growth over time; 182,000 was accurate earlier in 2026 but the current figure is ~187,000.
**Recommendation**: Update to "187,000+ GitHub stars (as of August 2026)" and note the as-of date explicitly in the citation/note so it doesn't go stale silently again.

---

**Claim**: OpenClaw/ClawdBot "gained 85,000+ GitHub stars in its first week" (January 2026)
**Verdict**: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED — 85,000 was a real intermediate milestone, but it understates the commonly-cited "viral surge" figure, and "first week" is imprecise/likely wrong framing.
**Sources**:
- [CNBC: From Clawdbot to Moltbot to OpenClaw (2026-02-02)](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/02/openclaw-open-source-ai-agent-rise-controversy-clawdbot-moltbot-moltbook.html) — reports the project "collected over 145,000 GitHub stars and 20,000 forks" as of publication (Feb 2, 2026).
- [HackerNoon: OpenClaw's 85,000 GitHub Stars Hide a Security Nightmare, Researchers Warn](https://hackernoon.com/openclaws-85000-github-stars-hide-a-security-nightmare-researchers-warn) — the actual origin of the doc's "85,000" figure; this was a security-focused report citing an intermediate star count at time of writing, not a "first week" total.
- [byteiota: OpenClaw Hits 369K GitHub Stars in 5 Months](https://byteiota.com/openclaw-hits-369k-github-stars-in-5-months-fastest-repo-ever/) — timeline: project went from 9,000 to 60,000+ stars in 72 hours in late January 2026 (the actual viral surge), reached 145,000 by early February 2026 (~1–2 weeks after the surge), surpassed React's 250,829 stars by March 3, 2026, and hit 369,000 by May 6, 2026.
**Contradictory evidence**: No source frames 85,000 as a "first week" total specifically; it appears to be a snapshot figure cited in one security report at an arbitrary point in the growth curve, and multiple sources use the 145,000 figure (reported ~1–2 weeks post-surge, closer to CNBC's early-Feb report) as the standard "viral launch" reference point.
**Recommendation**: Revise to the more commonly-cited, better-sourced figure. Corrected text: "In January 2026, ClawdBot (OpenClaw) went viral, growing from roughly 9,000 to over 60,000 GitHub stars in 72 hours and surpassing 145,000 stars within about two weeks — and was immediately found to have critical vulnerabilities..." Cite CNBC for the 145,000 figure and byteiota (or a similarly detailed timeline source) for the 72-hour growth detail if that level of specificity is wanted.
